abstract.t: RACR (Recipient-Authorized Content Retrieval, pronounced "racer") is a federated protocol for exchanging hail: recipient-authorized messages between portable identities. Stable decentralized identifiers identify participants independently of their current hosting providers. Signed authorization records and message envelopes use deterministic CBOR and COSE. A recipient provider validates authorization before retrieving a detached, digest-bound body from the sender provider. This document describes the architecture, core grant-authorized delivery, content profiles, privacy boundaries, and unresolved design issues of the current experimental protocol.

note.title: Editorial status
note.t: This is a first local working draft prepared for review. It has not been submitted to the IETF Datatracker, adopted by a working group, or approved as an RFC. Experimental is a proposed publication status, not an allocation of an RFC stream or a claim of IETF consensus.

This revision records the Hail alpha specification at repository commit d286113cd82024d009fb07cc60041f290047f148. Detailed semantic constraints still depend on that fixed specification snapshot. The document is not yet a self-contained replacement for those specifications. The open-issue appendix identifies work required before submission or a stable publication request.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: RACR separates permission to deliver a message from transport of its content. A recipient grants a particular sender permission to deliver selected categories of messages. The recipient provider remains authoritative for current permission, including revocation, even if the sender retains an older signed Grant. Senders publish immutable bodies and submit small recipient-specific signed envelopes. Recipients fetch content only after authenticating and authorizing an envelope.

The design aims to preserve recipient consent across provider changes, authenticate sending identities independently of their hosting domains, and avoid exposing user activity through message retrieval. It does not attempt to prevent abuse by a sender who has obtained consent, guarantee availability, or make provider-held message content end-to-end confidential.

RACR is not an SMTP or MIME profile, and an email-like address does not imply SMTP mailbox semantics. A gateway would require separately specified identity, consent, content-conversion, and failure rules. No such gateway is defined here.

The protocol remains an alpha design. Wire-version numbers select particular object formats, not a stability guarantee. An Internet-Draft revision number is unrelated to an RACR object version or an implementation release version.

section.name: Conventions and Scope
section.t: Hail names the communication medium; a hail is an individual recipient-authorized message. RACR names the underlying protocol that providers implement to exchange hail. Hail identifiers such as hail.envelope, application/hail-body+cbor, #hail-messaging, and HailMessaging name the objects, formats, keys, and services used by that protocol. They remain current identifiers, not deprecated names awaiting replacement. This terminology does not change wire bytes, signature domains, or interoperability requirements.

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

This draft specifies the architecture and summarizes normative core requirements from . Where a complete wire or semantic definition has not yet been incorporated, the corresponding specification in that pinned snapshot is a normative dependency. Editorial omissions in this draft do not create alternative encodings, relaxed validation, or new authority. Any inconsistency between the two documents is a defect to resolve before publication.

The core flow is delivery under a Grant using Envelope version 1. Connections, threaded replies, shared conversations, and provider transfer are implemented extensions, summarized in . They are not deferred merely because their complete definitions are outside this document. Implementations claiming an extension MUST implement its complete authorization and lifecycle rules.

A provider is infrastructure acting for one or more participant DIDs. A sender and recipient are protocol identities, not necessarily people. A Grant is a recipient-signed authorization lineage. An Envelope is a signed per-recipient delivery instruction. A Body is an immutable encoded content document. Acceptance is a durable authorization decision; delivery is durable storage of verified content and its recipient-specific message record.

section.name: Architecture and Trust Boundaries
section.artwork: Recipient Sender | | |-- discover address/profile ->| |-- publish signed Grant ----->| | | publish immutable Body |<-- submit signed Envelope ---| | authenticate; authorize | | atomically accept | |-- GET Body + bearer token -->| |<-- bounded content ----------| | verify; durably deliver | |-- signed delivery status --->|
section.t: There is one sender DID and one recipient DID per envelope. Multi-recipient delivery uses separate envelopes and authorization decisions, even when the body bytes are identical. A body digest is a content identity, not a message identifier or authorization credential.

HTTPS authenticates a network endpoint and protects data in transit. DID resolution establishes which keys and service endpoint currently act for a participant. COSE signatures bind protocol objects to a required key role. Recipient-local authoritative state determines whether the signed object authorizes an action. None of these checks substitutes for another.

Public address-to-DID and DID-to-service mappings are intentionally discoverable. Grant state, message state, account state, body-cache provenance, and user activity are protected. Privacy requirements therefore distinguish public routing information from relationship-dependent results.

section.name: Identity and Discovery
section.t: Current RACR DIDs use the exact lowercase syntax did:plc:[a-z2-7]{24}. A DID remains the durable identity when its hosting provider changes. A RACR address is a domain-verified alias; changing or withdrawing that alias does not revoke Grants issued to the DID.

A RACR DID document identifies distinct Ed25519 public keys at #hail-identity and #hail-messaging, and exactly one #hail service of type HailMessaging. The identity key signs Address Bindings and Grants. The messaging key signs Sender Profiles, Envelopes, and Delivery Status objects. Verifiers MUST check the exact key identifier, controller, algorithm, and role. A valid signature under another key of the same DID is insufficient.

The current key representation is Multikey using base58btc with the ed25519-pub multicodec prefix (0xed, encoded as bytes 0xed 0x01), followed by exactly 32 key bytes. The DID and PLC profiles, including resolution evidence and recovery trust, are defined in . General historical authority after recovery is an open issue in .

section.name: Address Bindings and Sender Profiles
section.t: An address uses a lowercase canonical ASCII local part and an IDNA A-label domain. Its local part permits dot-separated letter/digit/hyphen labels, is at most 63 bytes, and excludes quoting, comments, whitespace, non-ASCII characters, and domain literals. The complete canonical address is at most 254 bytes. These rules deliberately differ from SMTP mailbox syntax. The exact IDNA, DNS-delegation, and public-suffix checks remain in the Address Binding specification.

Discovery uses WebFinger with an acct URI . The client requires the exact canonical subject and exactly one matching link with extension relation https://hailproto.com/rel/address-binding and the COSE media type. The link relation uses the extension-URI mechanism of . The domain-selected HTTPS resource supplies a version-2 Address Binding signed by the named DID identity key. Neither a signature without domain publication nor domain publication without the signature verifies the address.

An Address Binding contains type, version, address, did, issued_at, and key_id. It has no expiration field and requires no periodic renewal. Current domain publication and current DID authority are nevertheless required. Cached verification lasts at most 3600 seconds, and is shortened by HTTP freshness, delegation TTLs, PLC policy, or local security policy. A retained signed binding does not justify indefinite verified-address display.

A prospective recipient retrieves Sender Profile version 2 from profiles/{sender_did} at the current sender service. The profile is signed by #hail-messaging and includes a revision, display metadata, offered categories, offers_uncategorized, and optional bounded bundled assets. Profile display metadata is not independent proof of an organization name. Grant creation binds the exact verified Address Binding and Sender Profile representation digests into consent_context.

section.name: Service URLs and Safe Fetching
section.t: A canonical RACR service base is an HTTPS URL with an ASCII DNS hostname, no credentials, query, fragment, IP-literal host, terminal DNS dot, or trailing slash. Default port 443 is omitted. Base-path segments permit only ASCII letters, digits, hyphen, dot, underscore, and tilde; empty interior segments and complete dot or dot-dot segments are invalid. The HTTP binding defines the limited permitted normalization of scheme, host, port, and a single trailing slash.

Operation URLs are constructed by appending one literal slash and the operation path to the canonical base. Generic relative-URI resolution MUST NOT replace the final base-path segment. A client MUST NOT follow redirects or forward bearer credentials to a redirect target. Provider changes are authenticated through DID resolution.

Cached discovery is refreshed once after the specified connection, redirect, not-found, gone, misdirected-request, or unknown-key conditions. A retry at a changed authenticated endpoint preserves the operation identity and required signed bytes. Body retrieval requires one sender-DID refresh after a concealed 404 before classifying authorization failure. Ordinary 429 and 5xx responses do not by themselves establish migration.

Outbound fetching MUST reject prohibited destinations and revalidate resolved addresses for each connection, preventing private-network access and DNS rebinding. Fetches require bounded time, bytes, and concurrency. A DID-authorized endpoint is not permission to reach arbitrary local networks.

section.name: Encoding, Signatures, and Digest Domains
section.t: RACR uses the core deterministic encoding requirements of CBOR . The data model permits null, booleans, integers from -(2^53-1) through 2^53-1, valid UTF-8 text, byte strings, finite arrays, and maps with unique text keys. Schemas further constrain values. Floating point, undefined, non-text map keys, indefinite lengths, application tags, duplicate keys, unknown fields in closed maps, and trailing bytes MUST be rejected.

Receivers perform bounded decoding, deterministic re-encoding, and byte-for-byte equality checking. Integers and lengths use shortest encodings; maps use encoded-key bytewise order. Text is not silently normalized. NFC requirements apply only where the schema specifies them. Diagnostic JSON is not a signed or hashed representation.

Signed objects use tagged COSE_Sign1 . Tag 18 is required. The protected map contains exactly labels 1 (alg), 3 (content type), and 4 (kid); the unprotected map is empty. The payload is embedded deterministic CBOR, external AAD is empty, and the signature is 64 bytes. alg is -19, the fully specified Ed25519 algorithm in ; polymorphic EdDSA value -8, negotiation, and fallback are not accepted. kid contains UTF-8 bytes of the canonical absolute DID key URL.

The protected content type is the exact object-specific string, such as application/hail-envelope+cbor. Together with the payload type, closed schema, fixed algorithm, and key role, it provides domain separation. The HTTP entity type is application/cose; cose-type="cose-sign1". HTTP media types are parsed according to their syntax, not compared as unparsed strings. Signed representations have no HTTP content coding.

li.t: Address Binding, Sender Profile, and Grant revision digests hash complete signed COSE representation bytes. A Grant predecessor and its ETag therefore change if its signature wrapper changes.
Envelope replay and Delivery Status correlation hash deterministic envelope payload bytes, excluding the COSE wrapper.
Body identity hashes exact uncompressed deterministic body bytes using SHA-256.

URL digest segments and bearer credentials use canonical unpadded base64url . A 32-byte digest renders as 43 ASCII characters. Content-Digest instead follows its structured-field syntax and hashes transferred content, including gzip coding when present.

section.name: Resource Budgets
section.t: All providers MUST support otherwise valid bodies through 1048576 encoded uncompressed octets. The budget includes CBOR framing and bundled asset data. It does not promise unlimited account quota or delivery capacity. Envelopes and Delivery Status representations are bounded at 16384 octets; Address Bindings at 16384 octets; Grants at 262144 octets. Other object-specific constraints remain applicable.

For independently decoded application CBOR domains, maximum depth is 32, total items 16384, array length 4096, map entries 256, and any text or byte string 1048576 bytes, subject to the overall encoded limit and stricter object limits. The root counts as one item at depth zero. Container elements, map keys, and map values count recursively; string contents do not. Map length counts pairs. Byte budgets include headers and use UTF-8 bytes rather than character counts.

For the outer COSE domain, depth is at most 8, total items 256, array length 8, map entries 8, and text length 1024 bytes; encoded and byte-string limits equal the object representation limit. Tag 18 counts as a root item and its array has depth one. Protected headers restart counting at their map with a 1024-byte encoded and byte-string limit and no tag. Embedded payloads are checked separately. Transfer snapshots have distinct limits and are not authorized by these budgets.
Implementations MUST bound allocation before trusting declared lengths. Wire-byte limits do not by themselves bound aggregate concurrent work or decoder scratch space.

section.name: Recipient Grants
section.t: Grant version 1 binds one grantor DID to one grantee DID, with a UUIDv7 grant_id , revision, predecessor digest, scope, status, timestamps, consent context, and identity key identifier. Scope contains exactly one selector: a nonempty set of offered categories, or uncategorized delivery. Uncategorized is not a wildcard. A Grant identifier is a lookup hint, not a bearer capability.

The recipient locally activates a Grant after explicit consent. Sender acknowledgment is not required for local activation, restriction, or revocation. The recipient latest revision is authoritative for delivery. The current profile permits one active Grant per grantor/grantee pair.

Every revision is a full-state snapshot. Revision 1 has a null predecessor. Subsequent revisions increment by one and name the SHA-256 digest of the previous complete signed representation. Type, version, grant_id, grantor, grantee, and issued_at are immutable within the lineage. Revision gaps, forks, conflicting representations, and changed immutable fields are rejected. Revocation is terminal for that lineage.

Expanding categories or switching categorized/uncategorized scope requires fresh explicit consent against current verified discovery evidence. Restriction or revocation MUST NOT depend on sender-profile availability and carries the previous consent context forward. A category omitted from the replacement snapshot is removed, not implicitly retained.

Before identity-key rotation, the current Grant revision is acknowledged by the grantee. Following rotation, the grantor issues a higher revision under the new key rather than re-signing the same revision. Unacknowledged-rotation recovery is unresolved; this draft does not authorize accepting stale keys merely to bridge that gap.

section.name: Publication and Conditional Updates
section.t: Grant publication is PUT grants/{grant_id} at the grantee service using the COSE entity type and no content coding. Revision 1 uses If-None-Match: * and no If-Match. A later revision uses one strong If-Match ETag whose opaque value is the base64url digest of the preceding complete signed representation, matching previous. Wildcards, weak tags, lists, and conflicting conditional fields are invalid for updates. HTTP conditional semantics follow .

Creation returns 201 with Location and ETag; an applied update or exact current update retry returns 204 with ETag. An exact creation retry returns 412 with the matching current ETag. Only an exact submitted-representation digest match makes that 412 idempotent convergence. Other conflicts require reconciliation. Responses use Cache-Control: no-store.

Before valid grantor authentication and local target confirmation, protected failures use a uniform 400 Problem Details result. Missing required preconditions may be disclosed as 428 only after authentication. Source-wide transport limits and public routing errors retain the independently selected exceptions defined in the HTTP binding. Grant publication does not permit querying unrelated relationships.

section.name: Core Envelope Delivery
section.t: A Grant-authorized Envelope version 1 contains type, version, message_id, from, to, authorization, created_at, expires_at, body, and reply; category and message_type have object-specific conditional semantics. authorization identifies type grant and the grant_id. The messaging signature authenticates from, which MUST equal the Grant grantee; to MUST equal the Grant grantor. The current category or uncategorized permission must authorize the message. The complete closed schema and conditional fields are defined by .

A body descriptor contains a SHA-256 digest, size from 1 through 1048576, media_type application/hail-body+cbor, profile spt-1/spt-2/spt-3, available_until, and bearer access metadata. available_until is at least created_at plus 2592000 seconds and expires_at plus 300 seconds. The access expiration is no earlier than available_until. The immutable body and its authorization MUST exist before envelope submission and be retained through that availability commitment.

POST envelopes submits one signed envelope. No additional federation authentication beyond HTTPS and COSE is required. Deployments may use private controls, but those controls do not replace protocol signature verification. Batch federation submission is not defined.

section.name: Validation and Atomic Acceptance

li.t: Enforce transport and representation limits, then bounded deterministic COSE and payload decoding, closed-schema validation, and inexpensive field relationships.

Use claimed fields only for privacy-safe preliminary rejection and the narrowly defined public DID routing check. A preliminary authorization miss MUST NOT trigger a body fetch or durable replay mutation.
Resolve and verify the exact sender messaging key and COSE signature. Authentication MUST precede protected detail, authenticated replay-state mutation, or body retrieval.

Serialize the authenticated (from DID, message_id) record. Identical payload digests reuse stored state; different payload digests conflict. Reserve authenticated rejection results as specified by the replay rules.

Atomically recheck current recipient authorization and policy, then persist accepted delivery and required capability state. Grant changes and acceptance share an ordering: a revocation committed first rejects the new message; acceptance committed first allows its body processing to continue.

Retrieve or reuse content only under the body authorization and provenance rules. Verify and stage it, then serialize the final deadline check, durable message publication, terminal state, and any capability consumption.

section.t: created_at cannot be more than 300 seconds in the future. The effective delivery deadline is the earliest of expires_at plus 300 seconds, body.available_until, and access.expires_at. Acceptance and durable delivery MUST occur no later than that deadline. Clock tolerance never extends body or token retention promises. If completion misses the deadline, the terminal result is failed with reason delivery-expired.

The replay key is the authenticated sender DID plus message_id, not the body digest. The sender MUST NOT reuse a message ID, including after rejection. Retained replay state lasts through at least max(expires_at, body.available_until) plus 300 seconds. Authenticated identical retries can recover stored state even after the original permission changes; they do not authorize a new delivery.

section.name: Submission Responses and Disclosure
section.t: Receipt, acceptance, and delivery are distinct. Before a sender is authenticated with a current or previous local relationship, protected outcomes use HTTP 202, Content-Type application/json without parameters, Cache-Control: no-store, and exactly the JSON object below. It contains no status-query handle or acceptance promise.

An eligible authenticated accepted or duplicate submission returns HTTP 200 with the current signed Delivery Status. Explicit protected errors map message-id-conflict to 409, invalid-envelope to 400, unauthorized to 403, message-expired to 410, rate-limited to 429, and temporarily-unavailable to 503. Every explicit unsuccessful response uses Problem Details without disclosing more than the caller is entitled to learn.

Relationship-independent method, media type, size, framing, and service-wide rate limits may return safe transport errors. A 421 is permitted only when sufficiently fresh authenticated public DID state proves an endpoint mismatch; local account or relationship absence does not justify it. Body retrieval has no public target DID and does not use this exception.

Concealed outcomes MUST have common status, response shape, privacy-relevant headers, and a bounded response schedule based on measured validation behavior. Implementations must bound network-dependent resolution and test repeated timing observations. A guessed constant delay alone is not evidence that rejection paths are indistinguishable.

section.name: Body Content and Retrieval
section.t: A body is a closed Safe Portable Text document, not arbitrary HTML. Every provider MUST validate, retrieve, and store spt-1, spt-2, and spt-3. Plain-text-only support is insufficient. spt-1 contains normal text blocks and unmarked spans. spt-2 adds specified headings, blockquotes, captions, lists, strong/em/code decorators, and declared HTTPS links. spt-3 adds exactly one leading image block referencing one bundled PNG header.

Clients MUST treat text as text, validate link schemes and attributes, and not interpret unknown nodes as executable markup. The current profiles define neither arbitrary HTML/CSS/scripts nor sender-controlled remote image loading. Advanced publisher layouts require new explicit nodes, validation, and presentation rules. A profile is not extensible merely because its data is represented as a map.

The header is limited to 196608 bytes, width 2400, height 1200, and 2000000 pixels. Asset size, digest, and PNG dimensions must agree with the bytes; animated PNG is prohibited. A message image requires plain-text alt text and may carry a caption, each at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes under the specified NFC and character rules. The complete body, including bundled bytes, still fits within 1 MiB. Sender Profile avatar limits are separately 32768 bytes, 512 by 512, and 262144 pixels.

These independent byte, pixel, and structural budgets do not allocate a future attachment allowance. General attachments, detached resources, and their per-resource and aggregate limits remain undefined.

section.name: Bearer Authorization
section.t: For each recipient envelope, the sender generates exactly 32 cryptographically random token bytes. The signed body descriptor carries the token, body identity, and expiry. A token may be reused for retries of the same envelope, but MUST NOT be reused for another recipient or unrelated envelope. The server stores a token digest associated with body digest, recipient, message, expiry, and active state.

GET bodies/{digest} sends Authorization: Bearer followed by the canonical unpadded base64url token, using the scheme syntax of without adopting OAuth issuance flows. Tokens MUST NOT appear in URLs. Possession authorizes retrieval: this mechanism does not prove possession of the recipient DID private key.

Missing, malformed, unknown, mismatched, inactive, or expired tokens receive uniform 404 responses that conceal body existence. An authorization-lookup outage also uses the concealed path. A missing or unavailable body may produce retryable 503 only after active token, digest, and expiry authorization has been established. After a 404 the recipient performs the required authenticated endpoint refresh before classifying failure.

Hashing token lookup records does not remove secrets from retained signed envelopes, outboxes, backups, or transfer history. Those copies need access controls and log redaction. A signature authenticates token bytes but does not encrypt them.

section.name: Content Verification and Compression
section.t: A successful retrieval returns 200 with application/hail-body+cbor and private, no-store caching policy. Receivers MUST support identity and gzip coding; gzip emission is optional. No other coding is defined. Gzip-coded input is limited to 2097152 octets. Decompression MUST enforce an output cap equal to the already-validated signed size, not merely check size after unbounded expansion. Streaming and bounded buffered implementations are both permitted.

After decompression, the recipient verifies exact signed length, SHA-256 digest, HTTP media type, profile, deterministic CBOR equality, and complete schema/resource validity before delivery. Content-Digest, when supplied, covers coded HTTP content and does not replace the signed uncompressed digest. Aggregate decompressor output, including concatenated gzip members, remains subject to the same cap.

A verified cache may avoid retrieval only for matching provenance (recipient DID, sender DID, body digest, media type, profile). Global storage deduplication MUST NOT change another recipient delivery path based on blob presence. Without matching provenance, a recipient-specific retrieval is required even if the underlying bytes already exist. This prevents probing cross-tenant content possession with deliberately unusable authorizations.
Retrieval is a provider delivery operation, not an open or read signal. Clients render verified local content rather than contact the sender when the user opens a message.

section.name: Delivery State and Status Reporting
section.t: The delivery states are accepted, on-hold, delivered, failed, and cancelled. Accepted fixes core Grant authorization and queues content processing; on-hold records a retryable impediment. Delivered means verified body and recipient-specific record are durable. Delivered, failed, and cancelled are terminal and cannot transition to another result. A terminal transaction prevents a concurrent retry from publishing a message after failure or cancellation. Later Grant revocation affects future acceptance, not already accepted Grant delivery.

Retryable reasons are sender-unreachable, body-temporarily-unavailable, body-transfer-interrupted, sender-rate-limited, and receiver-resource-constrained. Permanent failure reasons are body-authorization-failed, body-integrity-failed, body-invalid, body-unsupported, delivery-expired, and receiver-policy-rejected. Cancellation reasons are recipient-cancelled and receiver-administrative-cancellation. The recipient owns bounded retrieval retries and scheduling within the signed deadline.

Delivery Status version 1 is a complete signed snapshot with the original message ID, envelope payload digest, original sender and recipient, revision increasing by exactly one per created snapshot, state, and occurred_at. Accepted is revision 1; later states begin at revision 2. on-hold includes reason and retry_at; failure and cancellation include the appropriate reason; other states omit them. The status from is the original envelope to, and status to is the original envelope from. The original recipient messaging key signs it. retry_at is no earlier than occurred_at and no later than the effective delivery deadline. Other cross-field rules are fixed by the Delivery State specification.

PUT deliveries/{envelope_digest} pushes status to the original sender current service. The receiver verifies the original recipient signer and retained envelope correlation before disclosure or state mutation. HTTP 204 acknowledges a valid new revision, exact duplicate, or valid stale lower revision. Same-revision conflicts, impossible transitions, and higher revisions after terminal state are rejected. Unauthenticated or uncorrelated protected outcomes use the generic 202 and do not acknowledge delivery status. No federation status-query endpoint is defined.

Terminal status is attempted immediately. Nominal retry delays are 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, 1 hour, 6 hours, and then 24 hours. Each delay uses independent uniform integer jitter from ceil(0.8D) through floor(1.2D). For 429/503, the next delay is the later of local jitter and valid Retry-After, with remote guidance capped at 24 hours. The counter and absolute next-attempt time survive restart, generic receipts, and endpoint migration.

Absent acknowledgment or a specified permanent error, retries continue through at least max(envelope replay deadline, terminal occurred_at plus 2592000 seconds). The sender retains correlation records through at least the replay deadline plus 2592000 seconds. Key rotation can replace the status COSE wrapper around unchanged deterministic payload bytes without changing its revision. A delivery receipt does not attest client synchronization, display, opening, or reading.

section.name: Implemented Extensions and Deferred Features

li.t: Connections use deliberate invitation review, identity-signed confirmation, coordinator admission, and disconnect controls. Envelope version 2 carries unthreaded connection delivery. This is not an unsolicited inbox-request channel.

Envelope version 3 carries a signed parent for threaded direct replies, with either reply-capability or connection authorization. Current reply creation uses this format; historical unthreaded reply forms are not a mandatory compatibility baseline.

Fixed-roster shared conversations use descriptors, per-recipient Envelope version 4, Reply all, leave, expiry, and creator revival. V4 does not replace Grant-authorized Envelope v1. Connection and conversation permission is rechecked before retrieval and final delivery, unlike authorization fixed at core Grant acceptance.

Provider transfer uses authenticated handover, fencing, and current portable snapshot v7 / managed snapshot v8, connection checkpoint v3, and conversation checkpoint v1. Copying an export or retaining a signature does not grant live service authority. Its larger snapshot domains and signatures are separate from core COSE bodies.

section.t: The complete extension definitions are in the fixed snapshot . Their eventual division into companion Internet-Drafts is an editorial decision, not removal of implemented functionality. Local account APIs, CLI commands, passkey flows, database tables, and deployment topology are not federation requirements.

End-to-end encryption, general file attachments, additional publisher layouts, optional-profile capability discovery, bulk federation submission, and federated read/open receipts remain deferred. A provider-local implementation of an undeclared feature is not a negotiated interoperable extension.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The protocol relies on HTTPS authentication, Ed25519 signatures, SHA-256 integrity, secure random tokens, protected signing keys, and correct DID resolution. A recipient provider can inspect delivered content and metadata; a sender provider can inspect outgoing content and tokens. Neither provider authentication nor local disk/key encryption provides end-to-end confidentiality.

Identity and messaging keys have distinct authority. Compromise of a messaging key can impersonate its sender within available permissions. Compromise or provider custody of an identity key has broader consequences for Grants and bindings. PLC recovery and rollback can affect which keys are authoritative; this draft deliberately does not treat retained signature validity as a complete historical-authority proof.

Implementations MUST verify algorithm, key role, controller, protected content type, payload type, schema, and canonical bytes in addition to the signature. Closed maps and exact digest domains reduce ambiguity and cross-protocol confusion. Unknown versions require explicit rejection or their separately defined extension handling; they are not best-effort parsing opportunities.

Acceptance, revocation, replay reservation, reply consumption, cancellation, and terminal publication require atomic ordering. A valid signature does not resolve races. Incorrect transaction boundaries can create duplicate messages, bypass revocation, consume a capability more than once, or publish after a terminal failure.

Resource attacks include large declared CBOR lengths, deeply nested structures, expensive signatures, DID-resolution amplification, stalled transfers, gzip expansion, and image decoder attacks. Apply structural limits before expensive work; bound concurrent work and scratch allocation separately. Grants authorize delivery categories, not unlimited resource consumption.

Bearer tokens are transferable secrets. Store lookup digests and redact secrets from logs, but also protect signed representations and backups that necessarily retain raw tokens. Network redirects, ambient cookies, arbitrary URLs, and unsafe DNS resolution can exfiltrate tokens or reach private services; endpoint derivation does not remove the need for safe-fetch validation.

Retention and migration must preserve immutable bodies through their commitments, replay state through its deadline, and status evidence through retry/correlation windows. Storage deduplication cannot erase recipient-specific ownership and authorization. Operator recovery procedures require review beyond these wire requirements.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Public aliases, DID service entries, key history, and Sender Profiles allow identity correlation. A stable DID improves continuity but also links interactions across provider changes. DNS, directory operators, and providers can observe discovery and traffic metadata. HTTPS does not conceal those relationships from the services involved.

Generic receipts and concealed body errors reduce relationship and content-existence probing, but timing, response size, resolution latency, cache state, rate limits, and connection behavior can still disclose information. Implementations need measured tests of all rejection paths, not merely identical JSON. Public 421 routing decisions must remain independent of protected account and relationship state.

Signed delivery status exposes provider processing and availability, not user reading. Bodies and bundled images are fetched during delivery and rendered locally. User-initiated navigation to an HTTPS link can still disclose information to the destination; this is distinct from automatic content loading. Additional analytics or read-receipt extensions require separate privacy review.

Recipient-specific cache provenance is required even when physical bytes are deduplicated. Retained consent context and history improve auditability but contain relationships and content metadata; retention policies should minimize unnecessary copies without violating protocol continuity requirements.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This revision makes no registration request. The application/hail-*+cbor strings used in the alpha are provisional and are not claimed to be registered media types. They are nevertheless exact cryptographic domain-separation values in this profile. Implementations MUST NOT independently rename them. Final allocation will require coordinated wire and signature updates if the names change.

Before publication, the core media-type registrations need templates and expert review under and the structured-suffix rules of . Candidate core types are application/hail-address-binding+cbor, application/hail-sender-profile+cbor, application/hail-grant+cbor, application/hail-envelope+cbor, application/hail-delivery-status+cbor, and application/hail-body+cbor. The extension types need coordinated registration in their companion documents.

The existing application/cose media type, COSE_Sign1 tag, and COSE Ed25519 algorithm are reused without a new allocation. The address-binding relation is an extension relation URI, not a claim to a registered short relation token. The DID service type, DNS delegation convention, profile identifiers, reason-code extensibility, and future capability identifiers require an explicit registry review before stable publication. This paragraph does not establish new registries.

section.name: Implementation and Evaluation Status
section.t: The project includes a TypeScript reference provider, clients including a Rust CLI, and TypeScript and Go codec/vector implementations. Shared vectors exercise encodings, signatures, resource boundaries, and malformed inputs. Provider tests exercise delivery and persistence behavior. These are implementation evidence, not a complete security audit or independent-provider interoperability certification.

No particular implementation language or independently operated second provider is a prerequisite for circulating this draft. Review can begin with published schemas, vectors, and implementation behavior. Independent implementations and deployments would provide additional evidence. A full independent-provider trial is not claimed here.

Useful evaluation includes exact encoded body boundaries, multilingual and structured publisher content, bounded decompression, privacy timing tests, competing revocation/acceptance operations, replay after restart, endpoint migration, and storage failure after authorization. A client can preflight an encoded draft against size and structural limits; doing so cannot promise acceptance under dynamic authorization or quota policy.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation. These design goals make it different from earlier binary serializations such as ASN.1 and MessagePack.

This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049. It does not create a new version of the format.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: Fully-Specified Algorithms for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)

abstract.t: This specification refers to cryptographic algorithm identifiers that fully specify the cryptographic operations to be performed, including any curve, key derivation function (KDF), and hash functions, as being "fully specified". It refers to cryptographic algorithm identifiers that require additional information beyond the algorithm identifier to determine the cryptographic operations to be performed as being "polymorphic". This specification creates fully-specified algorithm identifiers for registered JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) polymorphic algorithm identifiers, enabling applications to use only fully-specified algorithm identifiers. It deprecates those polymorphic algorithm identifiers.

This specification updates RFCs 7518, 8037, and 9053. It deprecates polymorphic algorithms defined by RFCs 8037 and 9053 and provides fully-specified replacements for them. It adds to the instructions to designated experts in RFCs 7518 and 9053.

front.title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings

abstract.t: This document describes the commonly used base 64, base 32, and base 16 encoding schemes. It also discusses the use of line-feeds in encoded data, use of padding in encoded data, use of non-alphabet characters in encoded data, use of different encoding alphabets, and canonical encodings. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

This specification defines UUIDs (Universally Unique IDentifiers) -- also known as GUIDs (Globally Unique IDentifiers) -- and a Uniform Resource Name namespace for UUIDs. A UUID is 128 bits long and is intended to guarantee uniqueness across space and time. UUIDs were originally used in the Apollo Network Computing System (NCS), later in the Open Software Foundation's (OSF's) Distributed Computing Environment (DCE), and then in Microsoft Windows platforms.

This specification is derived from the OSF DCE specification with the kind permission of the OSF (now known as "The Open Group"). Information from earlier versions of the OSF DCE specification have been incorporated into this document. This document obsoletes RFC 4122.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.
This document defines a "problem detail" to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs.
This document obsoletes RFC 7807.

front.title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: Bearer Token Usage

abstract.t: This specification describes how to use bearer tokens in HTTP requests to access OAuth 2.0 protected resources. Any party in possession of a bearer token (a "bearer") can use it to get access to the associated resources (without demonstrating possession of a cryptographic key). To prevent misuse, bearer tokens need to be protected from disclosure in storage and in transport. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

This specification defines the WebFinger protocol, which can be used to discover information about people or other entities on the Internet using standard HTTP methods. WebFinger discovers information for a URI that might not be usable as a locator otherwise, such as account or email URIs.

This document defines the 'acct' Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) scheme as a way to identify a user's account at a service provider, irrespective of the particular protocols that can be used to interact with the account.
This specification defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web ("links") and the type of those relationships ("link relation types").
It also defines the serialisation of such links in HTTP headers with the Link header field.

front.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures

abstract.t: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

front.title: Additional Media Type Structured Syntax Suffixes

abstract.t: A content media type name sometimes includes partitioned meta- information distinguished by a structured syntax to permit noting an attribute of the media as a suffix to the name. This document defines several structured syntax suffixes for use with media type registrations. In particular, it defines and registers the "+json", "+ber", "+der", "+fastinfoset", "+wbxml" and "+zip" structured syntax suffixes, and provides a media type structured syntax suffix registration form for the "+xml" structured syntax suffix. This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes.

front.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures

abstract.t: This document proposes a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049). Its main goal is to provide an easy and unambiguous way to express structures for protocol messages and data formats that use CBOR or JSON.

section.name: Open Issues and Publication Work
section.t: This appendix is an explicit issue inventory, not permission for implementers to choose incompatible behavior. The current snapshot remains the implementation target while these questions are reviewed.

li.t: Historical authority: define acceptable evidence and reconciliation after PLC recovery or nullified branches, including unacknowledged Grant identity-key rotation. Retention of signed bytes alone does not settle authority at acceptance time.

Document completeness: incorporate or split the full object schemas, consent/category grammars, Sender Profile limits, address DNS-delegation and IDNA policy, status cross-field rules, and endpoint error matrices. Replace the monolithic repository reference with suitable standalone normative documents before seeking stable publication.

Resolver policy: distinguish the strict-public reference fresh-read/evidence policy from deployment choices, and establish the interoperability consequences of directory disagreement, caching, and recovery windows.
Registration: complete media-type templates, dependency/registry review, security review of the provisional names, and any coordinated transition required by assigned values.

Extension publication: select companion-document boundaries for connection admission, threaded replies, shared conversations, custody, and transfer; retain their current normative authority boundaries.

Content evolution: define new safe publisher-layout nodes and client presentation semantics. Define capability discovery and downgrade behavior only when optional profiles exist. The three current SPT profiles remain mandatory.

Attachments: specify resource identity, authorization, per-resource and aggregate byte/count budgets, availability, retry, delivery-completion, and retention semantics before introducing general attachments.

Submission preparation: review author metadata, intended status, IPR obligations, references, current draft date, and all unresolved editorial notes; run xml2rfc and idnits; then use the Datatracker submission tool. This draft has not been submitted.

section.name: Source Map and Review Boundary
section.t: The initial source snapshot is d286113cd82024d009fb07cc60041f290047f148. This document is maintained separately from the implementation specification. Its chapter mapping is: identity/discovery to did-profile.md, address-binding.md, sender-profile.md and plc-read-evidence.md; encoding to encoding.md and hail.cddl; Grants to grants.md; core delivery to core-delivery.md and envelopes.md; HTTP operations to http-binding.md; content to bodies.md and assets.md; state to delivery-state.md.

The deferred-feature inventory was checked against Questions That Can Be Deferred in core-delivery.md. Existing connections, shared conversations, and portability are described as implemented extensions. General attachments, advanced layouts, end-to-end encryption, and read receipts are not presented as existing capabilities.

Open issues distinguish editorial incorporation work from genuinely unresolved protocol decisions. In particular, current body size, mandatory SPT support, bearer body retrieval, Address Binding non-expiration, and permission ordering are already specified; they are not re-opened by this draft.

section.name: Body Structural Schema Excerpt
section.t: The following CDDL () is copied from the pinned hail.cddl body and asset definitions, with the digest dependency included. It defines structure only: the prose and source specification impose additional mark-reference, role, PNG, text, and cross-field validation. In particular, spt-3 permits exactly one header asset despite the reusable manifest allowing one or two entries. Unknown fields are not permitted.
